Hi everyone! I’m a mathematics student and I recently started using Lean while trying to formalize a new result I found in combinatorics.
While learning Lean I came across this community, and I really liked the idea behind the collaborative development of Lean and its libraries. So I thought I’d try to get involved and contribute something in combinatorics as well.
I’m still pretty new to Lean, so I’d ideally like to start with something small and manageable. Are there any open combinatorics topics that could be a good first project?
Also, if I manage to finish something useful, where would be the right place to contribute it / how does that usually work?
Thanks a lot, and great to meet you all!
Hello! For the last question, you can look at the contribution guide
Welcome! What topics are you interested in?
Thank you both for your replies :) I’m mostly interested in finite combinatorics and graph theory, with some interest in number theory too, but I’m quite open
The only thing I know about graph theory is that Mathlib needs more reviewers in that area :smile:

Filippo Cavallari said:

graph theory

Great! There are loads of stuff missing, but I think finding something to motivate you is the key :)
You could try:

  • In a preconnected graph, any two longest paths intersect
  • preconnected ↔ any new edge creates a cycle that uses that edge
  • p.IsPath ↔ p.toSubgraph.coe.IsAcyclic
  • There exists a path with length equal to G.ediam / G.radius / G.eccent v
  • Find the spectra of known graphs (completeGraph / pathGraph / starGraph)
  • (cycleGraph <| 2 * k + 3)ᶜ.cliqueNum = k
  • Define the Rado graph / Petersen graph and prove properties about it
  • Calculating the diameter of trees: G.IsTree → G.eccent u = G.edist u v → G.ediam = G.eccent v
  • docs#SimpleGraph.cycleGraph.cycle is an Eulerian walk (docs#SimpleGraph.Walk.IsEulerian)
  • In a preconnected graph with max-degree ≤ 2, any Eulerian walk is Hamiltonian

etc. Anything wink at you so far? Or do you perhaps have any theorems you know that you're wondering whether they exist? These are just stuff I think are missing, but if you play around with the API you'll probably find other missing lemmas pretty quick

Thanks! That’s really helpful. The first two caught my attention the most: they both sound interesting, and they also seem somewhat related, so I would be happy to start with one of those.
I’ll take a deeper look at the API, but since I don’t have another specific theorem in mind at the moment, I think one of these would be a good place to start.

I worked on the first two suggestions, and this is what I ended up with :)

I used the existing Walk/IsPath API for the longest-path result, and adj_and_reachable_delete_edges_iff_exists_cycle for the new-edge/cycle result. Both files compile without errors.

Does the overall approach look right? I would appreciate any feedback on what I could improve to make the code closer to mathlib’s standards.

New edge and cycles

import Mathlib.Combinatorics.SimpleGraph.Connectivity.Connected

namespace SimpleGraph

variable {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V)

/-- Two distinct nonadjacent vertices are reachable in `G` iff their new edge lies on a cycle after it is added to `G`. -/
theorem reachable_iff_exists_cycle_sup_edge {u v : V} (huv : u ≠ v)
    (hnadj : ¬ G.Adj u v) :
    G.Reachable u v ↔
      ∃ (w : V) (p : (G ⊔ edge u v).Walk w w), p.IsCycle ∧ s(u, v) ∈ p.edges := by
  have hdel : G.deleteEdges {s(u, v)} = G := by simpa using hnadj
  have hadj : (G ⊔ edge u v).Adj u v := by simp [sup_adj, edge_adj, huv]
  simpa [hadj, deleteEdges_sup, hdel] using
    (adj_and_reachable_delete_edges_iff_exists_cycle (G := G ⊔ edge u v) (v := u) (w := v))

/-- A graph is preconnected iff every missing edge lies on a cycle when it is added. -/
theorem preconnected_iff_forall_exists_cycle_sup_edge :
    G.Preconnected ↔
      ∀ ⦃u v : V⦄, u ≠ v → ¬ G.Adj u v →
        ∃ (w : V) (p : (G ⊔ edge u v).Walk w w), p.IsCycle ∧ s(u, v) ∈ p.edges := by
  constructor
  · intro hG u v huv hnadj
    exact (reachable_iff_exists_cycle_sup_edge (G := G) huv hnadj).mp (hG u v)
  · intro hcycles u v
    by_cases huv : u = v
    · subst v
      exact Walk.nil.reachable
    · by_cases hadj : G.Adj u v
      · exact hadj.reachable
      · exact (reachable_iff_exists_cycle_sup_edge (G := G) huv hadj).mpr (hcycles huv hadj)

end SimpleGraph

Longest paths intersect

import Mathlib.Combinatorics.SimpleGraph.Connectivity.Connected

namespace SimpleGraph

variable {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}

namespace Walk

/-- Paths whose supports meet only at their joining endpoint concatenate to a path. -/
private theorem IsPath.append {a b c : V} {p : G.Walk a b} {q : G.Walk b c}
    (hp : p.IsPath) (hq : q.IsPath)
    (hinter : ∀ z, z ∈ p.support → z ∈ q.support → z = b) : (p.append q).IsPath := by
  rw [isPath_def, support_append, List.nodup_append']
  refine ⟨hp.support_nodup, hq.support_nodup.tail, ?_⟩
  apply List.disjoint_left.mpr
  intro z hzp hzq
  have hzb := hinter z hzp (List.mem_of_mem_tail hzq)
  subst z
  have hnodup := hq.support_nodup
  rw [← q.cons_tail_support, List.nodup_cons] at hnodup
  exact hnodup.1 hzq

end Walk

/-- There is a path between two walk supports meeting each support only at its corresponding endpoint. The proof chooses a shortest connector. -/
private theorem exists_path_between_supports {a b c d : V} (hG : G.Preconnected)
    (p : G.Walk a b) (q : G.Walk c d) :
    ∃ x ∈ p.support, ∃ y ∈ q.support, ∃ r : G.Walk x y,
      r.IsPath ∧
        (∀ z, z ∈ r.support → z ∈ p.support → z = x) ∧
        (∀ z, z ∈ r.support → z ∈ q.support → z = y) := by
  classical
  -- Minimize over all endpoint choices, not just paths between the original starting vertices.
  have hex : ∃ n : ℕ, ∃ (x y : V) (r : G.Walk x y),
      x ∈ p.support ∧ y ∈ q.support ∧ r.IsPath ∧ r.length = n := by
    obtain ⟨r, hr⟩ := hG.exists_isPath a c
    exact ⟨r.length, a, c, r, p.start_mem_support, q.start_mem_support, hr, rfl⟩
  obtain ⟨x, y, r, hx, hy, hr, hlen⟩ := Nat.find_spec hex
  have hmin {x' y' : V} (s : G.Walk x' y') (hx' : x' ∈ p.support)
      (hy' : y' ∈ q.support) (hs : s.IsPath) : r.length ≤ s.length := by
    rw [hlen]
    exact Nat.find_min' hex ⟨x', y', s, hx', hy', hs, rfl⟩
  refine ⟨x, hx, y, hy, r, hr, ?_, ?_⟩
  · intro z hzr hzp
    by_contra hzx
    have hshort := r.length_dropUntil_lt_length hzr hzx
    have hbound := hmin (r.dropUntil z hzr) hzp hy (hr.dropUntil hzr)
    omega
  · intro z hzr hzq
    by_contra hzy
    have hshort := r.length_takeUntil_lt_length hzr hzy
    have hbound := hmin (r.takeUntil z hzr) hx hzq (hr.takeUntil hzr)
    omega

/-- Any two paths of globally maximum length in a preconnected graph have a common vertex. The graph does not need to be finite: existence of the two maximum-length paths is assumed explicitly. -/
theorem Preconnected.longest_paths_intersect {a b c d : V} (hG : G.Preconnected)
    {p : G.Walk a b} {q : G.Walk c d} (hp : p.IsPath) (hq : q.IsPath)
    (hpmax : ∀ (u v : V) (s : G.Walk u v), s.IsPath → s.length ≤ p.length)
    (hqmax : ∀ (u v : V) (s : G.Walk u v), s.IsPath → s.length ≤ q.length) :
    ∃ z, z ∈ p.support ∧ z ∈ q.support := by
  classical
  by_contra hdisj
  have hsep (z : V) (hzp : z ∈ p.support) (hzq : z ∈ q.support) : False :=
    hdisj ⟨z, hzp, hzq⟩
  obtain ⟨x, hx, y, hy, r, hr, hrp, hrq⟩ := exists_path_between_supports hG p q
  have hxy : x ≠ y := fun hxy ↦ hsep x hx (hxy.symm ▸ hy)
  have hrpos : 0 < r.length :=
    Nat.pos_of_ne_zero (fun hzero ↦ hxy (Walk.eq_of_length_eq_zero hzero))
  obtain ⟨p₁, p₂, hp₁, hp₂, hpeq⟩ := hp.mem_support_iff_exists_append.mp hx
  obtain ⟨q₁, q₂, hq₁, hq₂, hqeq⟩ := hq.mem_support_iff_exists_append.mp hy
  have hp₁sub : p₁.support ⊆ p.support := by
    rw [hpeq]
    exact p₁.support_subset_support_append_left p₂
  have hp₂sub : p₂.support ⊆ p.support := by
    rw [hpeq]
    exact p₁.support_subset_support_append_right p₂
  have hq₁sub : q₁.support ⊆ q.support := by
    rw [hqeq]
    exact q₁.support_subset_support_append_left q₂
  have hq₂sub : q₂.support ⊆ q.support := by
    rw [hqeq]
    exact q₁.support_subset_support_append_right q₂
  -- Any appropriate pair of pieces can be joined through the connector without repetition.
  have hjoin {u v : V} {s : G.Walk u x} {t : G.Walk y v}
      (hs : s.IsPath) (ht : t.IsPath) (hsp : s.support ⊆ p.support)
      (htq : t.support ⊆ q.support) : (s.append (r.append t)).IsPath := by
    apply hs.append (hr.append ht (fun z hzr hzt ↦ hrq z hzr (htq hzt)))
    intro z hzs hzrt
    rcases (Walk.mem_support_append_iff r t).mp hzrt with hzr | hzt
    · exact hrp z hzr (hsp hzs)
    · exact (hsep z (hsp hzs) (htq hzt)).elim
  have hfirst := hpmax _ _ (p₁.append (r.append q₁.reverse))
    (hjoin hp₁ hq₁.reverse hp₁sub (by simpa using hq₁sub))
  have hsecond := hqmax _ _ (p₂.reverse.append (r.append q₂))
    (hjoin hp₂.reverse hq₂ (by simpa using hp₂sub) hq₂sub)
  -- The two new paths use each original piece once and the positive-length connector twice.
  simp only [Walk.length_append, Walk.length_reverse] at hfirst hsecond
  have hplen : p.length = p₁.length + p₂.length := by rw [hpeq, Walk.length_append]
  have hqlen : q.length = q₁.length + q₂.length := by rw [hqeq, Walk.length_append]
  omega

end SimpleGraph

very cool! nice work :) i can't speak fully to code quality (still learning myself), but as a start there are some parts of the last proof which can be simplified using mathlib's tactics fully — definitely don't read this as criticism though, these are just the kinds of things that have helped me (i've commented in the proof where i've changed things)

"golfing"

import Mathlib.Combinatorics.SimpleGraph.Connectivity.Connected

namespace SimpleGraph

variable {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}

private theorem Walk.IsPath.append {a b c : V} {p : G.Walk a b} {q : G.Walk b c}
    (hp : p.IsPath) (hq : q.IsPath)
    (hinter : ∀ z, z ∈ p.support → z ∈ q.support → z = b) : (p.append q).IsPath := sorry

private theorem exists_path_between_supports {a b c d : V} (hG : G.Preconnected)
    (p : G.Walk a b) (q : G.Walk c d) :
    ∃ x ∈ p.support, ∃ y ∈ q.support, ∃ r : G.Walk x y,
      r.IsPath ∧
        (∀ z, z ∈ r.support → z ∈ p.support → z = x) ∧
        (∀ z, z ∈ r.support → z ∈ q.support → z = y) := sorry

theorem Preconnected.longest_paths_intersect {a b c d : V} (hG : G.Preconnected)
    {p : G.Walk a b} {q : G.Walk c d} (hp : p.IsPath) (hq : q.IsPath)
    (hpmax : ∀ (u v : V) (s : G.Walk u v), s.IsPath → s.length ≤ p.length)
    (hqmax : ∀ (u v : V) (s : G.Walk u v), s.IsPath → s.length ≤ q.length) :
    ∃ z, z ∈ p.support ∧ z ∈ q.support := by
  -- `classical` wasn't necessary here
  -- `by_contra!` (with `!`) pushes the negation inside, which recovers what you did manually for `hsep`
  by_contra! hsep
  obtain ⟨x, hx, y, hy, r, hr, hrp, hrq⟩ := exists_path_between_supports hG p q
  have hxy : x ≠ y := fun hxy ↦ hsep x hx (hxy.symm ▸ hy)
  -- using `obtain` with `rfl` substitutes along the equality, which avoids the `rw [hpeq]` etc
  obtain ⟨p₁, p₂, hp₁, hp₂, rfl⟩ := hp.mem_support_iff_exists_append.mp hx
  obtain ⟨q₁, q₂, hq₁, hq₂, rfl⟩ := hq.mem_support_iff_exists_append.mp hy
  have hjoin {u v : V} {s : G.Walk u x} {t : G.Walk y v}
      (hs : s.IsPath) (ht : t.IsPath) (hsp : s.support ⊆ (p₁.append p₂).support)
      (htq : t.support ⊆ (q₁.append q₂).support) : (s.append (r.append t)).IsPath := by
    apply hs.append (hr.append ht (fun z hzr hzt ↦ hrq z hzr (htq hzt)))
    intro z hzs hzrt
    rcases (Walk.mem_support_append_iff r t).mp hzrt with hzr | hzt
    · exact hrp z hzr (hsp hzs)
    · exact (hsep z (hsp hzs) (htq hzt)).elim
  -- since we `subst`-ed along `p = p₁.append p₂`, `simp` can discharge the goals
  -- here which needed `hp₁sub` and friends
  have hfirst := hpmax _ _ (p₁.append (r.append q₁.reverse))
    (hjoin hp₁ hq₁.reverse (by simp) (by simp))
  have hsecond := hqmax _ _ (p₂.reverse.append (r.append q₂))
    (hjoin hp₂.reverse hq₂ (by simp) (by simp))
  -- `lia` (a specialisation of `grind`) is nowadays preferred to `omega`.
  -- if you want to go all-in on automation, `grind` can take care of `hplen`, `hqlen`,
  -- `hrpos` and the `simp [...] at hfirst hsecond` with a little suggestion.
  grind [Walk.length_append, Walk.length_reverse]

end SimpleGraph

the overall proof idea looks pretty good to me! the only thing i wonder is whether exists_path_between_supports to something with signature

theorem exists_path_between_sets (hG : Preconnected G) (s t : Set G) :
    ∃ x ∈ s, ∃ y ∈ t, ∃ r : G.Walk x y, r.IsPath ∧
      (∀ z, z ∈ r.support → z ∈ s → z = x) ∧ (∀ z, z ∈ r.support → z ∈ t → z = y) := sorry

or even

theorem exists_path_between_sets (hG : Preconnected G) (s t : Set G) :
    ∃ x ∈ s, ∃ y ∈ t, ∃ r : G.Walk x y, r.IsPath ∧ (s ∩ r.support = {x}) ∧ (t ∩ r.support = {y}) := sorry

since you don't use the walks themselves, just their support. if it stays a private theorem that matters less i suppose.

Filippo Cavallari said:

I worked on the first two suggestions, and this is what I ended up with :)

Could you please clarify if and how you've used LLMs for the code/message? Thanks!
btw you can use Pairwise fun u v ↦ instead of ∀ ⦃u v : V⦄, u ≠ v →

Thanks for the feedback! The point about the helper makes sense to me. For now I’m mainly trying to learn, so I’ll keep working on this privately until I have a stronger grasp of Lean.
I use Codex to explore mathlib’s API and try to understand where I make mistakes.
So the above code is entirely manually written?

Well not entirely, like the block using adj_and_reachable_delete_edges_iff_exists_cycle

simpa [hadj, deleteEdges_sup, hdel] using
    (adj_and_reachable_delete_edges_iff_exists_cycle (G := G ⊔ edge u v) (v := u) (w := v))

has been suggested by Codex when I was exploring the API.

That could be replaced with

simp [← adj_and_reachable_delete_edges_iff_exists_cycle, edge_adj, huv, hdel]

and hadj is then redundant.

LLMs can give bad advice when you're starting out, and if your goal is to learn then I'd advise against using them in favor of asking questions on #new members or getting PR reviews.
For example I'd guess that all the omegas in your code came from an LLM? You shouldn't use omega, try lia instead.
Also there are lots of haves and obtains, which is usually either because an LLM wrote it, or following a natural language argument in a book, or just not being used to backwards reasoning yet.

I haven't read through carefully yet, but I find it surprising that you have to use Nat.find here. Could you try docs#Set.Finite.exists_minimal instead?

Actually those omegas were mine: I saw them used in the proof of IsCycle.isPath_take in one of the related PRs. After reading your message, I looked into it and realised that lia is preferred now.

I’ll also look into Set.Finite.exists_minimal and see whether I can simplify the proof structure and remove some intermediate steps. I’ll definitely take your advice and ask here when I get stuck. Thanks for taking the time to help :)

Oh we should definitely fix that, sorry!
